```{r, include = FALSE}
options(rmoriebricklayer.xmssidxfile = tempfile())
# chunks run when the vignette is built (R CMD build, r-universe, pkgdown) and are skipped when
# R CMD check re-builds it (R sets _R_CHECK_PACKAGE_NAME_ there), unless NOT_CRAN is true
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true") ||
                        !nzchar(Sys.getenv("_R_CHECK_PACKAGE_NAME_")))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(rmoriebricklayer)
```

A capsule is only as trustworthy as the signature on its manifest. `rmoriebricklayer`
implements the three NIST post-quantum signature standards natively, with no system
cryptography library: **ML-DSA** (FIPS 204, lattice-based), **SLH-DSA** (FIPS 205,
hash-based, stateless) and **XMSS** (RFC 8391, hash-based, stateful). All three are used
through the same two calls, `cpssign()` and `cpsvrf()`.

## Why post-quantum, and why three schemes

A signature made today may need to verify in twenty years, when a large quantum computer
could break RSA and ECDSA with Shor's algorithm. The three schemes rest on different
assumptions, so a break of one does not take the others:

* **ML-DSA** (Module-Lattice Digital Signature Algorithm, formerly Dilithium) rests on the
  hardness of Module-LWE and Module-SIS. Small keys and signatures, fast. The default.
* **SLH-DSA** (Stateless Hash-based, formerly SPHINCS+) rests only on the security of a hash
  function. Conservative; its signatures are large.
* **XMSS** is also hash-based but *stateful*: every key signs a fixed number of times and
  an index must never be reused. The package carries the state forward for you.

## ML-DSA: the default

```{r mldsa}
key <- fipskg("ML-DSA-65")
key$scheme

sig <- cpssign("a manifest digest", key)
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", sig, fipspubkey(key))
```

The verifier needs only the public key. Any change to the message is caught:

```{r mldsa-tamper}
cpsvrf("a manifest digest (edited)", sig, fipspubkey(key))
```

### Context strings bind a signature to its purpose

FIPS 204 lets a signature carry a *context*: a short string hashed in with the message. The
same message signed for one purpose does not verify under another, which stops a signature
made for "staging" being replayed as a "release" approval:

```{r context}
sig2 <- cpssign("a manifest digest", key, ctx = "release")
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", sig2, key, ctx = "release")
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", sig2, key, ctx = "staging")
```

### Hedged and deterministic signing

By default ML-DSA signing is *hedged*: fresh randomness enters every signature, so two
signatures of one message differ (FIPS 204 recommends this; it also protects against
fault attacks on the nonce). `deterministic = TRUE` gives the variant where the signature
depends only on the key and the message:

```{r deterministic}
s1 <- cpssign("same message", key, determ = TRUE)
s2 <- cpssign("same message", key, determ = TRUE)
identical(s1$signature, s2$signature)

h1 <- cpssign("same message", key)
h2 <- cpssign("same message", key)
identical(h1$signature, h2$signature)
```

### Signing a digest computed elsewhere

ML-DSA signs `mu = H(tr || M')`, a digest of the message that depends on the public key but
not on the secret. `fipsmu()` computes it from the *public* key, so the machine holding the
secret never needs to see the message:

```{r mu}
mu <- fipsmu(fipspubkey(key), "a manifest digest", ctx = "release")
sig3 <- fipssignmu(key, mu)
fipsvrfmu(key, mu, sig3)
# the same signature verifies the ordinary way
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", sig3, key, ctx = "release")
```

Since 0.5.10, ML-DSA signing runs **first-order masked** by default (see the
*Side-channel assurance* vignette): every secret-dependent value is held as two random
shares. The signatures are byte-identical to the unmasked computation; only the cost differs.

## SLH-DSA: hash-based, stateless

```{r slh}
fipssz("ML-DSA-65")
fipssz("SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f")
```

The price of dropping the lattice assumption is size: an SLH-DSA signature is far larger
than an ML-DSA signature at the same security level.

```{r slh-size}
fipssz("SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f")[["signature"]] > fipssz("ML-DSA-44")[["signature"]]
```

The calls are identical:

```{r slh-sign}
hkey <- fipskg("SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f")
hsig <- cpssign("a manifest digest", hkey)
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", hsig, fipspubkey(hkey))
```

### Pre-hash variants

HashML-DSA and HashSLH-DSA sign a digest of the message instead of the message itself,
for very large inputs or when the message is hashed on another machine. The hash
function's OID is bound into the signature, so two digests of the same length never
verify for each other:

```{r prehash}
p <- cpssign("a large artifact", key, prehash = "sha512")
cpsvrf("a large artifact", p, key, prehash = "sha512")
cpsvrf("a large artifact", p, key, prehash = "sha3_512")
```

## XMSS: hash-based, stateful

An XMSS key of height *h* signs 2^h messages. The package stores the next index in the key
and `xmssadv(key, signature)` gives the advanced key after every signature; reusing an index would break security,
so always advance the key with `xmssadv()` and save that:

```{r xmss}
xkey <- pqckg(height = 3)
xkey$capacity
xkey$next_index

s1 <- cpssign("manifest-1", xkey)
cpsvrf("manifest-1", s1, signpubkey(xkey))

xkey <- xmssadv(xkey, s1)
xkey$next_index
s2 <- cpssign("manifest-2", xkey)
cpsvrf("manifest-2", s2, signpubkey(xkey))

# a signature does not transfer to another message
cpsvrf("manifest-1", s2, signpubkey(xkey))
```

The key is a value, so an old copy of it still says an old `next_index`. The package therefore
also keeps a record of the highest index each key has used on this machine (`?xmssadv`
says where), and refuses a used index even from a stale copy. A key generated here is entered
at birth; a key from another machine, one rebuilt from its seeds, or one used in a CI job or a
container with a fresh home directory is unknown to the record and must be vouched for once
with `xmssregkey(key)` before it signs from index 0.

### The key file is the state

RFC 10033 (*Hash-Based Signatures: State and Backup Management*) separates the private key,
which never changes, from the state, the indices already used, which must be updated and
saved before a signature is released, and warns that a copied or restored state signs used
indices again. `rmbl sign` follows it: with `--scheme xmss-sha256 --key-file key.json` the key
file is the state. It is rewritten atomically, with `next_index` advanced and a `used` field,
before any bundle is written, and the run signs from the indices it reserved.

```{r xmss-cli}
root <- tempfile("capsules-")
for (nm in c("one", "two")) {
  d <- file.path(root, nm)
  dir.create(d, recursive = TRUE)
  utils::write.csv(data.frame(x = 1:3), file.path(d, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
  writeLines('{"resource": {"filename": "data.csv"}}', file.path(d, "data_provenance.json"))
}
kf <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
writeLines(tojs(unclass(pqckg(height = 4)), auto_unbox = TRUE), kf)
copy <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
invisible(file.copy(kf, copy))   # an old copy of the key, kept by mistake

status <- blcli(c("sign", root, "--scheme", "xmss-sha256", "--key-file", kf, "--json"),
                out = function(s) NULL)
status
state <- fromjs(paste(readLines(kf), collapse = "\n"))
state$next_index                # two capsules signed, two indices used
state$used$generation

# the old copy is refused: the bundles show indices it does not know are used
blcli(c("sign", root, "--scheme", "xmss-sha256", "--key-file", copy, "--overwrite"),
      out = function(s) cat(s[grepl("stale", s)]))
xmssidxseen(root)[, c("index", "reused")]
```

`--state-file` keeps the state in a file of its own. `--sectors K --sector-index I` splits the
indices into K disjoint ranges so that K signers can share one key, each in its own range
(RFC 10033, section 5.3), and `--reserve N` marks N indices used in one write and signs from
them (section 5.9; the ones a run does not use are lost). A key kept as a CI secret is a
fixed copy that every job starts from, so every job would sign the same indices: in CI, sign
with ML-DSA unless the XMSS state lives in a file that persists between jobs. NIST SP 800-208
approves XMSS only inside a hardware module that never exports the key, which a key file is
not.

## Every way of being wrong returns FALSE

Verification returns `FALSE` for every signature of the right shape that does not verify: a
truncated or edited signature, a foreign key and an edited message all fail the same way.
(An object that is not a signature at all, a key of the wrong class or a missing message
is an error, because that is a programming mistake rather than a tampered artefact.)

```{r wrong}
pub <- fipspubkey(key)
bad <- sig
bad$signature <- paste0("ff", substring(bad$signature, 3))
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", bad, pub)
trunc <- sig
trunc$signature <- substring(sig$signature, 1, 64)
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", trunc, pub)
cpsvrf("a manifest digest", sig, fipspubkey(fipskg("ML-DSA-65")))
```

## How these implementations are checked

ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are compared byte for byte with OpenSSL 3.5 and run against the NIST
ACVP and C2SP Wycheproof vector sets on every change (6,848 checks, 0 failures at 0.5.10),
and fuzzed differentially against OpenSSL; XMSS, which OpenSSL does not implement, is
checked against the RFC 8391 vectors. Every signer runs under valgrind with the secret key
marked undefined, a dynamic check that no executed branch or memory address depends on it. `SECURITY.md` in the package
repository has the full table of what each check catches and what it does not.


## Signing a release of Indigenous tables

A signature lets anyone check that a release came from its publisher and has not
changed:

```{r indigenous-sign}
key <- fipskg("ML-DSA-65")
d <- indiex("mentalhealth")
msg <- dgstobj(d)
sig <- cpssign(msg, key)
cpsvrf(msg, sig, fipspubkey(key))
```

## The sizes in a picture

What a signature costs on the wire, from `fipssz()`: the public key a verifier keeps and the
signature attached to each release, in bytes, for ML-DSA and two SLH-DSA sets. The scale is
logarithmic, because an SLH-DSA signature is several times larger.

```{r signature-sizes-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
sch <- c("ML-DSA-44", "ML-DSA-65", "ML-DSA-87", "SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f", "SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s")
sz <- t(vapply(sch, function(s) fipssz(s)[c("public_key", "signature")], numeric(2)))
op <- par(mar = c(9, 5, 3, 1))
barplot(t(sz), beside = TRUE, log = "y", ylim = c(10, 2 * max(sz)), col = blpal()[1:2],
        ylab = "bytes (log scale)", las = 2, cex.names = 0.8, legend.text = c("public key", "signature"),
        args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bty = "n"), main = "Key and signature sizes")
par(op)
```
